Cohesion: how it fits together

70 diagrams. Each diagram has Fit width / 100% / zoom / Full screen controls. Sources are Mermaid blocks in docs/tour/*.md.

Part A: The product

A1. What Cohesion is, as a product

One person, one daemon, many screens. Everything the person owns lives in a single database on the machine that runs cohesiond; every app is just a window onto it. Agents and extensions are the two ways the system does things on its own.

A2. Who talks to whom (runtime topology)

Four kinds of party: the daemon, ordinary clients, edge clients (a client that also serves the daemon), and the outside world. The thick arrows are the paired, authenticated links.

A3. What your data looks like (the content model)

Tables that matter to a person, and how they relate. Workspace is the container for your work; agents, feeds, accounts and devices sit outside any one workspace.

A4. What lives outside any workspace: intelligence and agent data

Part B: Inside the daemon

B1. The parts of cohesiond, and the threads they run on

CohesionContext (in cohesionkit) is the bag of handles every request handler gets. Everything is a cheap clone around shared state. The one thing that is not async is the database: a single OS thread owns the SQLite connection.

B2. Crate layering (what may depend on what)

One-way dependencies. The CLI never links SQLite, QuickJS or the LLM code. A lower crate that needs something from a higher one declares a tiny trait (ConnectorAccess, ServiceAccess, EdgeInference) and the higher crate implements it.

B3. Daemon startup, in order

B4. One request, end to end (the canonical request flow)

Example: you tick a task as done in the web UI. The same path serves every command from every client.

B5. Which kind of Route handles a command?

#[derive(Commands)] on Command generates dispatch. Each variant says which kind of route it uses; the default is Database.

B6. Inside the database worker: why every command is atomic and observable

B7. Live updates: how every screen stays in sync

The server never pushes data, only what is now stale. Clients refetch what they are showing.

Invalidation keys (what "stale" can mean)

Part C: Clients, identity and pairing

There is no username or password anywhere. A client is a row in the clients table, identified by how it proved itself before the session began: a TLS certificate fingerprint (key_kind = certificate) or a local key hash (key_kind = local). A client has no "type"; whether it is also an edge client is just whether it sends an Offer.

C1. The family of clients

C2. Pairing a new device (remote, over the network)

A setup key exists only during a pairing window: it dies after one registration or ten minutes. The setup code is base64("key|ip|server-fingerprint"), so it carries the secret, where to connect and which server key to expect.

C3. Local clients on the Unix socket

No TLS here. The socket file's permissions are the trust.

C4. The web UI path: cohesion open

The browser has no identity of its own. A loopback proxy owned by the CLI lends it the CLI's.

C5. What happens when you delete a client (revoke a device)

Part D: Events, hooks and time

Nothing in Cohesion polls your data. When a command commits, it can raise a database event; the HookManager turns that (and wall-clock ticks) into hook events on one ordered queue; the HookReceiver runs them one at a time, first in extensions, then in agents' cues. This is the "what wakes it up" for everything automatic.

D1. The event bus

D2. Journal "settling" (why journal:settled is delayed)

A journal is saved on every pause while you type. Waking an agent on each save would be absurd, so the save only restarts a timer.

D3. The day clock

D4. Loop protection: why agents and extensions can't wake each other forever

Every database event carries a trace: a depth counter plus an origin (which extension or which agent wrote). A write made while handling an event continues that trace.

Part E: Agents

An agent is a persistent assistant: one standing conversation, a short status line, and cues (hooks that wake it up in the background). It is not a long-running process. Between events it is just rows in the database; a thread to a model is built when something needs it.

Two modes, with deliberately different powers:

Foreground (chat) Background (a cue's run)
Started by you: message, choice pick, reaction a hook event whose cue predicate returns truthy
Model the agent tier's default the tier named by the cue's effort (low / medium / high)
Script pool foreground_agents: read-write cohesion, network, connectors, storage, agent background_agents: read-only cohesion, connectors, services (readOnly fns), backgroundAgent, writable storage, no network
May change data yes, on the strength of your message no: may only set status, propose, or message you
Can set cues / pin yes no

E1. Anatomy of an agent (what is stored, who uses it)

E2. "User creates an agent"

Note what is not chosen at creation: the model. An agent has no model of its own; it uses whatever the agent tier points at at the time of each turn.

E3. "User sends a message": the foreground turn

The request returns immediately (AcceptedResponse); the turn runs on its own task. Clients follow it through invalidations: the status flips to working, messages land in the feed as the agent's tools post them.

E4. What the model "remembers": context, pins and the rolling thread

The model's thread is disposable. What survives is the feed (database) plus pins and storage.

E5. An agent sets a cue ("what wakes it up")

A cue is a (hook, predicate-script, instructions, effort) tuple. The agent writes it from inside the chat by running a script that calls agent.cue(...).

E6. A cue fires: the background run

This is the whole "something happened, so the agent wakes and acts" path. Cheap first (a JS predicate on a small pool), expensive only if it passes (an LLM call).

E7. Proposals: how a background run is allowed to change anything

A proposal is a message containing code. The code runs only after you press Approve, with write access, on the foreground pool.

E8. State machines

E9. Choices and reactions (the lightweight ways to talk to an agent)

Part F: Inference (how a model gets chosen and called)

Four ideas, in order of indirection:

  1. An endpoint is where a model runs: an HTTP provider account (Anthropic, OpenAI, an OpenAI-compatible server) or an edge endpoint (a device).
  2. An endpoint model is which model that endpoint offers, optionally linked to a catalog model (models.dev) for price and context size.
  3. A tier (agent, low, medium, high) is a named slot that points at exactly one endpoint model.
  4. A session never names a model. It asks for a tier, at the moment it starts.

F1. The indirection chain

Deleting a model or an endpoint unsets the tiers that used it (database cascade), so a tier can be empty; asking an empty tier fails with NoDefaultModel.

F2. "User sets up inference"

F3. "Which model does this run use?" (decision flow)

F4. One model turn, inside Session

Session is the conversation engine for every model use; agents are just callers with particular tools and system prompts.

F5. Tools available to each kind of session

Part H: Extensions, connectors and scripts

An extension is one JS/TS file with a manifest() and some hook functions. It is the way to add behaviour without changing Rust: react to events (hooks), expose callable functions (services), sign you in to outside services (OAuth accounts), import items (connectors), offer other extensions to install (registries), or run on a timer.

Trust rule: an extension is trusted once installed and a grant is on. Everything starts off. A grant decides which mounts (JS globals) its sandbox gets; nothing inside a mount second-guesses the grant.

H1. Lifecycle of an extension

H2. Script sandboxes: who gets which globals

Every script runs on a dedicated thread in a fresh QuickJS runtime; scopes never share prototypes. What differs is the pool and the mounts.

Quick reference of the permission → mount map (Mount::for_permission):

Permission Mount / effect
cohesion:read, cohesion:write cohesion global (write makes the guard writable and hook arguments writable)
network network
timer timer
oauth accounts; daemon may call the sign-in functions
services services (call other extensions' declared functions)
usage usage
registry, connector, service, service:isolated no global: they let the daemon (or clients) call certain functions in the extension

H3. A hook reaching an extension (concurrency detail)

H4. Services: extensions calling each other, and clients calling extensions

H5. Connectors: adding an account (OAuth) and importing

An extension holding oauth + connector is a connector. The daemon calls its sign-in and import functions.

Part K: Putting it all together

K1. The master map: every moving part and the arrows between them

Read this once, then use Parts A to J as zoom-ins. Letters in brackets point at the part that expands each box.

K2. A whole story: "Tell me when something urgent lands"

One timeline touching clients, DB, hooks, cue evaluation, inference tiers, the edge call, a proposal, and the phone. Every step maps to a diagram above.

K3. The same story, with tier low pointed at the Mac's on-device model (what happens TODAY)

The wire protocol already carries the tool definitions to the device, but the macOS shim answers without tools: its LanguageModelSession has none, and the model has a 4,096-token window while the background code tool alone is roughly 12,000 tokens (see docs/edge-measurement.md). So a background run on the device can read the wake message and write text, but it cannot call send_message, run code or propose. The model's final text lives only in the run's thread; the user sees nothing.

Practical reading: today an edge intelligence offer is best for measurement and plain-text uses. Giving devices tools (the "tool bridge") is deliberately waiting on those measurements and on your go-ahead.
